extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors, technical founders, and expert-level innovators considering a DIY prior art search
extracted.subtask_description: Step-by-step guidance for inventors/innovators to perform an effective prior art search themselves using free online patent databases and non-patent literature, plus when to hire a patent lawyer and how to document findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether you should do the search yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide if you are qualified to perform a prior art search yourself based on your technical expertise and familiarity with the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are an expert-level innovator generally familiar with existing work in your field, you are probably qualified to do your own prior art search. If you lack extensive experience in the technical field, hire a professional searcher or patent attorney. Even if you can do the search yourself, you'll likely need a patent attorney later to develop strategy and analyze patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the goals/benefits of conducting a prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the search to inform patent decisions and reduce downstream problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key benefits listed: avoid submitting patent applications with claims that are not patentable and will be easily rejected; determine whether your invention is novel; develop a strong patent claim strategy before filing (reduce chance of extensive amendments); account for close prior art in drafting by describing advantages or improvements to support non-obviousness; understand how your idea fits into the technological field; be better prepared to discuss your invention with a patent attorney and explain what aspects might be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brainstorm comprehensive keywords to describe the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate all possible keyword combinations that could appear in prior art so you don't miss relevant documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for reasons other patents/applications may use unusual keywords: industry terminology changes over time, different industries use different keywords for similar concepts, many patent filings are translated into English. Aim to capture synonyms, older/newer terms, cross-industry vocabulary, and translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search major patent databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Query multiple free patent search tools to find patent documents relevant to your keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended tools: Google Patents, USPTO search interface, Espace (European Patent Office) search interface, WIPO search interface, Patent Lens. The page explicitly recommends these as starting points and implies using several sources rather than relying on a single database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer keyword-driven searches and top-results review over relying on patent classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not primarily rely on the USPTO classes/subclasses system; instead use keyword searches and inspect top hits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many practitioners find the USPTO classification system is not particularly useful for prior art searching. Recommended method: make a list of the top 10 patent documents for each keyword and then explore citations and referenced documents from those top hits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform forward-and-backward (citation) cross-reference searching
rubrics_metrics.description: For each relevant patent document, look at patents it cites (backward) and patents that cite it (forward) to discover related prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to do this in Google Patents: open the patent page, scroll to the bottom, review 'Patent Citations' and 'Referenced By' sections, scan titles for relevance and click links to review. In USPTO interface: view the document, scroll to 'References Cited' for backward references and look for 'Non-Patent Citations'. This technique helps find related documents that keyword searches may miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expand search beyond patent documents to non-patent literature (NPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Search scholarly publications, product pages, commercial listings, and other public disclosures because prior art includes any publicly available disclosure, not just patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested NPL sources: Google Scholar for scholarly publications; non-patent literature such as articles, journals (printed or electronic); Amazon or other commercial sites; product pages of companies that might be innovating in the same space. The list is not exhaustive — consider theses, conference materials, and foreign-language sources as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save and organize all relevant results and documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a comprehensive, organized record (e.g., spreadsheet and full-document copies) of relevant prior art you locate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing a patent application you will want to cite the most relevant prior art to the USPTO. Save a list of relevant results and complete copies of documents to ensure you can cite them and to satisfy ethical duties of disclosure, candor, and good faith. The page recommends using a spreadsheet to track references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and satisfy ethical duties of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you disclose prior art that could affect patentability when filing, fulfilling duties to the patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner has the most relevant references, you'll often end up with a stronger patent. Saving and citing relevant prior art ensures you satisfy ethical duties of disclosure, candor, and good faith to report prior art that could affect claim patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know when to stop searching—seek sufficient, not exhaustive, coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop when you have enough prior art to understand where your invention stands; exhaustive coverage is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to gain a comprehensive understanding of the invention's standing in the industry, not to find every possible document. Factors that make completeness impossible include the 18-month publication window (some prior art may not yet be public) and unindexed or obscure documents (e.g., academic theses, foreign-language documents). Use experience and common sense to decide when to stop.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you find prior art, assess its effect and adjust patent strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering prior art does not necessarily invalidate a patent claim; analyze how the reference affects claim scope and what steps can overcome it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page advises that finding prior art can be discouraging but may not invalidate the entire patent. Consider how prior art affects different types of claims and consult resources or a patent attorney for strategies to overcome obstacles (e.g., drafting differences, claiming distinguishing features, or focusing on inventive improvements). The firm offers an eBook covering these strategies.
